The problem with AI contributions isn't the AI, it's the lack of human in the loop aspect of it, nobody wants vibe coded bugfixes that you might never come back to work on if there's issues or regressions once its merged.
I don't like that there's blind AI hate, and blind AI love, I am one of the few somewhere in the middle, who just wants to use it in a useful way.
All that said, I don't blame him.
I think it's to the point you're almost better off submitting the suggested bug fix to maintainers if you're using AI and leaving it to them if they so would accept such a bug report.

In retrospect, it should be no surprise to us that Claude is sandbagging. Why? Because Anthropic
wrote the paper on how to do it without getting detected
:
https://alignment.anthropic.com/2025/automated-researchers-s...
They found that they were able to reduce automated research performance without increasing suspiciousness (to the monitor model), by both prompting the research model to imitate a weaker model and providing examples of sandbagging.
From their paper:
> Simply using a weaker model like Claude 3 Haiku achieves much lower task performance at a low suspiciousness score. In principle, imitating weaker models would thus be an effective sandbagging strategy. However, we were not able to effectively elicit this strategy with zero-shot prompting [..] Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieves its best sandbagging performance when prompted to imitate a weaker model and given a one-shot example of effective subtle sandbagging. comments.author: mrob
comments.text: IMO, any system that was exploited by this was already insecure. It's not exploiting bugs in the inference engine or attempting any kind of sandbox escape. Here the exploit was in the chat template, but it's possible to encode the same thing directly in the weights. Unless the model is truly Open Source (not just open weight), there's no way to know what malicious instructions might be encoded in the weights. The only defense is to sandbox the agent sufficiently strongly that it can't do harm no matter what tokens it generates. In such a sandbox, it doesn't matter that the payload was stored directly in the GGUF file, because it won't be able to do anything with it anyway.

For a good few decades (1950s-1980s), the US and the soviet union seemed locked into an unstoppable race of developing ever more devastating nuclear weapons. Fission bombs, high-yield fission bombs, boosted fission, thermonuclear warheads, MIRV, ICBMs. Eventually, both sides achieved "overkill", the ability to completely erase human civilization using their stockpiles. And humanity got really closed to being wiped out this way at least once.
Still, and despite the immense political tensions between the two superpowers at the time, we managed to pull ourselves back from the brink and avoid nuclear holocaust. We stopped developing even stronger nuclear weapons before the most terrible plans such as Sundial were realized. We even achieved some moderate success in reducing the existing stockpiles.

comments.author: amluto
comments.text:
> Depth-wise cross-attention (split Q/K/V): While standard transformer attention operates across tokens in a sequence, DCA applies attention across layers in depth. Each token queries a dynamically weighted mix of all prior layer embeddings, unlocking the model's full historical context without the computational penalty usually required to scale traditional attention.
I’ve often thought that something like this might lead to a real solution to the infamous strawberry problem.
Ignoring pesky issues like tokenization, the actual input data is visible to the model as the embedding fed to the first layer, but the first layer is probably nowhere near smart enough to understand that the model is trying to count R instances.  But by the time whatever layer is reached that might understand the goal, the non-wasteful part of the low-level memory (the K’s and V’s from the first layer) can’t be queried any more.
But this cross-depth attention can query them!
Admittedly, there are holes in this argument.  Beyond just tokenization (to the extent that the model can see letters at all, it is reconstructing them), the attention mechanism doesn’t really have a clean “count the hits” operation.

comments.author: smallerize
comments.text: If it's an independent project, you shouldn't be using the same name without an explicit sign-off from the original project. It's rude to confuse users that way, plus it might be actual trademark infringement.

comments.author: Octoth0rpe
comments.text:
I'm a bit of a monospace font snob and I like this quite a bit. A couple of observations:
- in the example text, the `{i}` and `[l]` look quite odd to me. The bottom of the braces fall below the baseline, but the tops don't extend as far above the characters proportionally (especially noticeable on the l).
- Looks a _little_ to thick for my tastes, but maybe a light variant would help. The thickness particularly hurts the lowercase r.
- kerning looks a little rough in some uppercase combinations, see `GH`, `MN`, `CD` (I only checked the standard alphabet ordering, not a list of known problematic combinations.
- rough lowerspace combinations: `fg`, `jk` look a little too far apart
